title: 道德經 第八十一章
source: Laozi 老子, 道德經 (Daodejing), chapter 81, in the Wang Bi 王弼 recension (華亭張氏原本, 晉 王弼注), as transcribed at Chinese Wikisource; verified character-for-character against the printed public-domain edition of Paul Carus, Lao-Tze's Tao-Teh-King: Chinese-English (Chicago: Open Court, 1898), p. 93. All punctuation is editorial — the original has none — and the division into 81 chapters is traditional. Sense-units follow Wang Bi's own commentary lemmata. Translations are made fresh from the Chinese. Pronunciation convention: modern Mandarin, given in Hanyu Pinyin — an admitted anachronism, and the living convention for reading these texts. Where an Old Chinese rhyme is invisible in Mandarin, a note says so. Prepared audio is synthesized speech in that same convention (cmn-CN-Chirp3-HD-Achernar).
about: Chapter 81 of the Daodejing. Its traditional title is 顯質 (Showing What Is Plain). The chapter titles are not part of the text and are not Wang Bi's: they come from the Heshanggong 河上公 recension and are carried here only as navigation labels, so a chapter can be found by something other than its number. The received text is Wang Bi's (3rd c. AD); the manuscripts found at Mawangdui (1973) and Guodian (1993) are older and differ in places, and the notes flag those differences where they matter. Classical Chinese has no inflection, no obligatory subject, and no fixed parts of speech — the notes show how the line produces its meaning. Read the characters; the pinyin under each one is a reading aid you can hide with the transcription button.

morph.gloss: trustworthy, as good as one's word; true to the fact

sentences.i: Words to be trusted are not fine words;
sentences.n: The last chapter of the book is three couplets of this shape, then three lines on the sage, then a closing pair. Each half of a couplet is four characters with no verb 'to be' in it: 'trustworthy words | not beautiful'. The predication is made by putting the two things side by side, and 不 negates the adjective directly. Note that a noun would be negated by 非 instead — 非常道 in chapter 1 — while 不 goes with verbs and adjectives; the choice of negator tells you what part of speech the writer had in mind.

sentences.i: fine words are not to be trusted.
sentences.n: The second half turns the first inside out: 信 and 美 trade jobs. What was the subject's quality becomes the predicate, and what was the predicate becomes the subject; nothing else moves. This is the book's commonest figure, and in a language with no inflection it costs nothing to make: the same four characters, in the other order.

sentences.t:
善者不辯，
辯者不善。
知者不博，

morph.gloss: the one who — makes a noun of what precedes it
to argue a case, to plead, to be eloquent in dispute
broad, wide-ranging — of learning, the man who has read everything

sentences.i: A good man does not plead his case; the man who pleads is not good. One who knows is not a man of broad learning;
sentences.n:
者 after a verb or adjective makes a noun of it: 善者 'the one who is good', 辯者 'the one who argues'. It is the nearest thing the language has to an ending, and it attaches to whole phrases as readily as to single words — you met it in 兩者 'the two of them' back in chapter 1.

辯 is not conversation; it is pleading, the art of winning an argument, and 辯者 became the standing name for the professional disputants of the Warring States. 博 is the opposite fault to 知: knowledge that has spread wide instead of going down.

The Mawangdui manuscripts order these couplets differently and read the 善 pair as 善者不多，多者不善, with 多 'much' where the received text has 辯 'argue' — 'the good man has not much; the man who has much is not good', which pairs the line with 聖人不積 below rather than with the pleading.

sentences.t:
博者不知。
聖人不積，

morph.gloss: the sage — in this book the ruler who holds the Way, not a moral saint
to heap up, to store, as grain is stored in a barn

sentences.l:
the wide-learned one does not know.
The sage does not hoard.
sentences.i: the man of broad learning does not know. The sage stores nothing up.
sentences.n: 積 is the granary word — heaping up against a future. Four characters, and then the chapter spends two whole lines explaining why the sage can afford not to.

morph.gloss: for the sake of, on behalf of (wèi — the benefactive reading; see the note)
self, himself — the answering term to 人 'others'

sentences.l: Having already used it for others, he himself has all the more;
sentences.i: The more he lays out on others' behalf, the more he has;
sentences.n:
為 is read wèi here, and this is the exception the house rule names. 為 is wéi — do, make, act, count as — everywhere in this book except where it takes a plain noun in a benefactive sense, 'for the sake of', which is wèi: 為人 has no action-word after it, only the people it is done for. Compare 為腹不為目 in chapter 12, also wèi.

己 and 人 are a fixed pair, 'self' against 'others', and the couplet turns entirely on it. 愈 is 'all the more'. The construction has no 'if' and no 'the more … the more' — just two clauses laid side by side, and you supply the hinge.

morph.gloss: to give, to hand over (yǔ — in chapter 79 the same character was 'to side with')
much, many — here as a verb, 'to be abundant, to have much' (the answering term to 有 'to have' in the line above)

sentences.l: having already given it to others, he himself is all the more abundant.
sentences.i: the more he gives away, the more he is left with.
sentences.n: The couplet does not repeat itself: the first line ends in 有 'has', this one in 多 'is much'. 與 is 'to give' here — two chapters back, at the end of 79, the same character was 'to be on the side of'. One graph, two words, and only the sentence tells you which.

morph.gloss: to benefit, to do good to

sentences.l:
The way of heaven:
benefits, and does not injure;
sentences.i: Heaven's way brings gain and never injury;
sentences.n: 利 and 害 are a standing pair — profit and injury, the two things a man reckons before he acts. Both are used here as verbs with no stated object: heaven benefits, and does not harm, and whom is left open because the answer is everything.

sentences.t:
聖人之道，
為而不爭。

morph.gloss: the sage — in this book the ruler who holds the Way, not a moral saint
to contend, to fight for place, to compete

sentences.l:
the way of the sage:
acts and does not contend.
sentences.i: the sage's way is to act and never to compete.
sentences.n:
The last line of the book, and worth pausing on. 為 is wéi, 'to act' — after eighty chapters of 無為, acting without forcing, the closing word is not that the sage does nothing. He acts. What he does not do is compete, and the whole of 無為 turns out to have been about the second half of that, not the first.

The Mawangdui manuscripts read 人之道, 'the way of man', for 聖人之道, and 弗爭 for 不爭 — 弗 being generally analysed as 不 with its object already absorbed into it, 'does not contend over it'.

One more thing about where you are standing. In the received text this ends the book. In the Mawangdui manuscripts the two halves are in the other order — the 德 chapters (38–81) come first and the 道 chapters (1–37) after — so this chapter sits in the middle of the oldest substantially complete copies we have, and the book ends at what we number 37. (The Guodian slips are older still, but they are a selection, not a whole book.) The 81-chapter arrangement you have just read to the end of is an editor's, not the author's.
